claims.claim: Mid-frontal theta oscillations (3–8 Hz) have been identified as a reliable marker of mnemonic conflict specifically.
claims.source: On a neurophysiological level, mid-frontal theta oscillations (3–8 Hz) have been identified as a reliable marker of cognitive conflict in general (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014) and mnemonic conflict specifically (Ferreira et al., 2014; Hanslmayr et al., 2010; Johansson et al., 2007; Staudigl et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferreira et al., 2014; Hanslmayr et al., 2010; Johansson et al., 2007; Staudigl et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Increased theta amplitudes may facilitate the emergence of phase separation, where populations of neurons transmitting potentially interfering information are segregated in time along a theta cycle.
claims.source: Increased theta amplitudes may facilitate the emergence of phase separation, where populations of neurons transmitting potentially interfering information are segregated in time along a theta cycle (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004.

claims.claim: Computational models assign a central role to the phase of the hippocampal theta oscillation in the ordered representation of multiplexed information.
claims.source: On a theoretical level, computational models assign a central role to the phase of the hippocampal theta oscillation in the ordered representation of multiplexed information (Lakatos et al., 2005; Lisman, 2005; Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Nyhus and Curran, 2010; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple computational modeling studies.

claims.claim: In rodents, bursts of gamma power reflecting sequences of spatial information processing are represented at different phases of the hippocampal theta oscillation.
claims.source: Empirically, in rodents it has been shown that bursts of gamma power reflecting sequences of spatial information processing are represented at different phases of the hippocampal theta oscillation (Bragin et al., 1995; Colgin et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bragin et al., 1995 and Colgin et al., 2009.

claims.claim: In humans, neural representations of items held in working memory or encoded into or retrieved from episodic memory cluster at distinct phases of the (hippocampal) theta rhythm.
claims.source: Several recent studies in humans suggest that the neural representations of items held in working memory or encoded into or retrieved from episodic memory (Kerrén et al., 2018; Kunz et al., 2019; Pacheco Estefan et al., 2021) cluster at distinct phases of the (hippocampal) theta rhythm.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kerrén et al., 2018; Kunz et al., 2019; Pacheco Estefan et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Low-frequency oscillations provide time windows for the selective processing and readout of distinct units of information.
claims.source: These findings suggest that low-frequency oscillations provide time windows for the selective processing and readout of distinct units of information (Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lisman and Jensen, 2013.

claims.claim: The oscillating interference resolution model leverages different phases of a theta oscillation to iteratively differentiate target from competitor memories.
claims.source: One computational model leverages different phases of a theta oscillation to iteratively differentiate target from competitor memories (Norman et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Norman et al., 2006.

claims.claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, a retrieval cue will activate associated units, representing target and competitor features, in a phase-dependent manner.
claims.source: In this model, which we will henceforth refer to as the oscillating interference resolution model, a retrieval cue will activate associated units, representing target and competitor features, in a phase-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model from Norman et al., 2006.

claims.claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, at medium levels of inhibition, the cue only activates the target units and no or few competitor features.
claims.source: In the most desirable output state, at medium levels of inhibition, the cue only activates the target units and no or few competitor features.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claims.claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, when inhibition is raised towards the peak of the oscillation, only strong features of the target memory will remain active.
claims.source: When inhibition is raised towards the peak of the oscillation, only strong features of the target memory will remain active, and the model learns (via contrastive Hebbian learning) to strengthen through long-term potentiation (LTP) the weaker target nodes that did not survive the higher inhibition levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claims.claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, the model learns to strengthen through long-term potentiation (LTP) the weaker target nodes that did not survive the higher inhibition levels.
claims.source: When inhibition is raised towards the peak of the oscillation, only strong features of the target memory will remain active, and the model learns (via contrastive Hebbian learning) to strengthen through long-term potentiation (LTP) the weaker target nodes that did not survive the higher inhibition levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claims.claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, during the transition from a medium to a lower inhibition state towards the trough of the oscillation, activation spreads to more weakly associated units, including some competitor features.
claims.source: Conversely, during the transition from a medium to a lower inhibition state towards the trough of the oscillation, activation spreads to more weakly associated units, including some competitor features.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claims.claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, the opposite phase is used to identify and punish overly strong features of the competing memory through long-term depression (LTD).
claims.source: This opposite phase is used to identify and punish overly strong features of the competing memory through long-term depression (LTD).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claims.claim: The oscillating interference resolution mechanism is repeated across several cycles of an oscillation, which changes the similarity structure of memories into a state in which they are less likely to interfere with each other.
claims.source: The mechanism (see Figure 1) is repeated across several cycles of an oscillation, which changes the similarity structure of memories into a state in which they are less likely to interfere with each other.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model and references Figure 1.

claims.claim: A previous study provided proof-of-principle evidence that the reactivation of a single visual memory is rhythmically modulated by the hippocampal theta rhythm.
claims.source: A previous study (Kerrén et al., 2018) provided proof-of-principle evidence that the reactivation of a single visual memory is rhythmically modulated by the hippocampal theta rhythm.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kerrén et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Target and competitor memories become active, and can thus be decoded, at different phases of the hippocampal theta oscillation.
claims.source: Based on the oscillating interference resolution model (Norman et al., 2006) and related theta-gamma models (e.g., Lisman and Idiart, 1995), we expected that target and competitor memories become active, and can thus be decoded, at different phases of the hippocampal theta oscillation, with only target features active at higher inhibition phases, and competitors surfacing as inhibition ramps down to medium and low levels (see Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis derived from the oscillating interference resolution model and related models, and references Figure 1d.

claims.claim: Across several repetitions of the theta cycle, weak features of target memories are strengthened while overly strong features of competing memories are punished to make them less interfering on future cycles.
claims.source: The model also assumes that across several repetitions of the theta cycle, weak features of target memories are strengthened while overly strong features of competing memories are punished to make them less interfering on future cycles.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the assumptions of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claims.claim: The effects of the oscillating interference resolution dynamics will become visible across several repetitions of competitive retrieval and lead to an increasing phase separation.
claims.source: We hypothesised that the effects of these dynamics will become visible across several repetitions of competitive retrieval and lead to an increasing phase separation because over time target memories become more likely to activate in the high-inhibition phase whereas competing memories require increasingly lower levels of inhibition to activate.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis derived from the oscillating interference resolution model.

claims.claim: The strengthening of target and weakening of competing memories should be reflected in corresponding changes in their decodability.
claims.source: Lastly, in line with previous literature (Wimber et al., 2015), the strengthening of target and weakening of competing memories should also be reflected in corresponding changes in their decodability.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by a citation to Wimber et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Memory performance was significantly reduced in the competitive (M = 53.18%, SD = 19.20%) compared to the single-exposure (M = 57.71%, SD = 13.98%) condition, t(23) = 1.80, p<0.05.
claims.source: The main planned comparison of interest showed that memory performance was indeed significantly reduced in the competitive (M = 53.18%, SD = 19.20%) compared to the single-exposure (M = 57.71%, SD = 13.98%) condition, t(23) = 1.80, p<0.05 (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Retrieving a memory is more difficult when a previously encoded, now irrelevant associate competes for recall, indicative of proactive interference.
claims.source: This confirms the first behavioural hypothesis (OSF) that retrieving a memory is more difficult when a previously encoded, now irrelevant associate competes for recall, indicative of proactive interference.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing reduced memory performance in the competitive condition.

claims.claim: A significant difference was obtained between NC1 and NC2 (M = 78.88%, SD = 10.06%), t(23) = –11.91, p<0.05, demonstrating that a second encoding exposure improved performance compared to a single exposure.
claims.source: A second post-hoc test showed that a significant difference was also obtained between NC1 and NC2 (M = 78.88%, SD = 10.06%), t(23) = –11.91, p<0.05, demonstrating that, unsurprisingly, a second encoding exposure improved performance compared to a single exposure.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: On trials where participants made an error, they showed a significantly above-chance (i.e. above 50%) probability of selecting the subcategory of the competitor (on average, 88.72%, SD = 10.62%; t(23) = 10.48, p<0.05).
claims.source: On trials where participants made an error (i.e. selected 'object' though the target was a scene and vice versa), they showed a significantly above-chance (i.e. above 50%) probability of selecting the subcategory of the competitor (on average, 88.72%, SD = 10.62%; t(23) = 10.48, p<0.05), suggesting that their errors were not random but biased towards the category of the previously learned but now irrelevant associate (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Participants' errors were not random but biased towards the category of the previously learned but now irrelevant associate.
claims.source: On trials where participants made an error (i.e. selected 'object' though the target was a scene and vice versa), they showed a significantly above-chance (i.e. above 50%) probability of selecting the subcategory of the competitor (on average, 88.72%, SD = 10.62%; t(23) = 10.48, p<0.05), suggesting that their errors were not random but biased towards the category of the previously learned but now irrelevant associate (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing above-chance selection of competitor subcategories.

claims.claim: The proportion of intrusions did not change significantly across repetitions (first: 88.08%, SD = 12.04%; second: 89.23%, SD = 10.62%; third: 88.85%, SD = 14.72%, Z = –54, p=0.59).
claims.source: The proportion of intrusions did not change significantly across repetitions (first: 88.08%, SD = 12.04%; second: 89.23%, SD = 10.62%; third: 88.85%, SD = 14.72%, Z = –54, p=0.59; Wilcoxon signed-rank test of linear slope against zero).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: There was no decrease across repetitions in behavioural accuracy for CC target items (Z = –0.73, p=0.47).
claims.source: Similarly, we did not find a decrease across repetitions in behavioural accuracy for CC target items (Z = –0.73, p=0.47; Wilcoxon signed-rank test of linear slope against zero; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: Across participants, the average number of intrusions in the CC correlated negatively with memory performance in the non-competitive conditions, r = –0.37, p=0.037, p<0.05.
claims.source: Across participants, the average number of intrusions in the CC correlated negatively with memory performance in the non-competitive conditions, r = –0.37, p=0.037, p<0.05 (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), indicating that better memory performance was generally associated with fewer intrusion errors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: Better memory performance was generally associated with fewer intrusion errors.
claims.source: Across participants, the average number of intrusions in the CC correlated negatively with memory performance in the non-competitive conditions, r = –0.37, p=0.037, p<0.05 (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), indicating that better memory performance was generally associated with fewer intrusion errors.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference from the negative correlation between intrusions and memory performance.

claims.claim: The average response time for subjective recollection was 2.11 s (SD = 0.15 s) when collapsing across all conditions and repetitions.
claims.source: The average response time for subjective recollection (indicated by button press) was 2.11 s (SD = 0.15 s) when collapsing across all conditions and repetitions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Response times shortened across repetitions in all three conditions (CC: rep1: 2.29 s, rep2: 2.05 s, rep3: 2.04 s; Z = –2.89, p=0.004; NC1: rep1: 2.55 s, rep2: 2.37 s, rep3: 2.26 s; Z = 3.03, p=0.003; NC2: rep1: 2.01 s, rep2: 1.75 s, rep3: 1.68 s; Z = –4.17, p<0.001).

claims.claim: A non-parametric cluster-based permutation test revealed a significant power increase when retrieving the target association in the CC compared to the NC2 condition (pcluster<0.05), ranging from approximately 500 to 700 ms post-cue.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2c.

claims.claim: In addition to behavioural evidence for proactive interference, we also replicate previous work that established frontal theta power increases as a neural signature of competition.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing theta power increases and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In terms of its topography, this frontal effect was more right-lateralised than the typically observed mid-frontal theta.
claims.source: Note, however, that in terms of its topography, this frontal effect was more right-lateralised than the typically observed mid-frontal theta (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014), and might instead be more related to response conflict or response inhibition (for a review, see Aron et al., 2004).

claims.claim: The reliable above-chance decoding performance was somewhat later than the typical time window for reinstatement of associative memories in cued recall tests.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data and a citation to Staresina and Wimber, 2019.

claims.claim: No significant cluster could be identified when correcting for multiple comparisons across time points in the CC, indicating that overall reinstatement was less robust in the condition where two associates competed for recall.

However, no significant cluster could be identified when correcting for multiple comparisons across time points, indicating that overall reinstatement was less robust in the condition where two associates competed for recall, potentially because this competition was associated with less confident target retrieval.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2e.

This method revealed two clusters of significant target classification preceding the button press by approximately 200 ms (Figure 2f).

claims.claim: A significant repetition-by-associate interaction was found (F(1,20) = 5.187, p=0.034), with a significant increase of target reactivation from first to third recall (first: 49.43%, SD = 4.08%; third: 53.14%, SD = 6.43%; t(20) = –2.46, p=0.02), and a numerical but non-significant decrease of competitor reactivation (first: 52.05%, SD = 4.55%; third: 50.82%, SD = 5.54%; t(20) = 1.1, p=0.29).

claims.claim: A significant correlation (r = 0.446, p=0.04) was found such that stronger reactivation of competitor memories positively correlated with a higher level of initial intrusions.
claims.source: Lastly, taking inspiration from previous work on competitor reactivation and its relationship to behavioural memory interference (Newman and Norman, 2010), we extracted the average decoding across repetitions for the competitor memories from 0 to 1 s after cue onset and correlated this reactivation with the probability of intrusions in the first repetition. claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

results.result: The study demonstrates behavioral evidence for proactive interference. Memory performance was significantly reduced in the competitive condition (CC: 53.18%) compared to the single-exposure condition (NC1: 57.71%), t(23)=1.80, p<0.05, confirming that retrieving a memory is more difficult when a previously encoded, now irrelevant associate competes for recall. A second encoding exposure (NC2: 78.88%) significantly improved performance compared to single exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 provide converging behavioral evidence for proactive interference with appropriate statistical tests and controls. The comparison between CC and NC1 directly tests the interference hypothesis, while NC2 serves as a control for encoding repetition effects. The statistical analyses are appropriate (paired t-tests) with significant p-values reported.

results.result: Participants' errors in the competitive condition were systematically biased toward competitor memories. On error trials, participants selected the competitor's subcategory 88.72% of the time (significantly above 50% chance, t(23)=10.48, p<0.05), indicating non-random intrusion errors. The proportion of intrusions remained stable across repetitions (p=0.59), and higher intrusion rates correlated with lower overall memory performance (r=-0.37, p=0.037).
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 demonstrate that errors reflect genuine memory competition rather than random guessing. The above-chance intrusion rate with strong statistical support (t=10.48) and the correlation with overall memory performance provide converging evidence. The stability of intrusions across repetitions is properly tested with non-parametric statistics appropriate for the data.

results.result: Response times for subjective recollection averaged 2.11s across conditions and shortened significantly across repetitions in all three conditions (CC: Z=-2.89, p=0.004; NC1: Z=3.03, p=0.003; NC2: Z=-4.17, p<0.001), indicating that memory retrieval became faster with repeated recalls.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 provide clear evidence for practice effects in memory retrieval. The use of Wilcoxon signed-rank tests is appropriate for testing linear trends, and the consistent pattern across all conditions with significant p-values supports the interpretation that retrieval speed improves with repetition.

results.result: Mnemonic competition was associated with increased frontal theta power (3-8 Hz) approximately 500-700ms post-cue when comparing CC to NC2 conditions (pcluster<0.05). However, this effect was more right-lateralized than typical mid-frontal theta and might relate to response conflict or response inhibition rather than mnemonic conflict per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 demonstrate a neural signature of competition using appropriate cluster-based permutation testing. The authors appropriately note the topographic difference from typical mid-frontal theta and acknowledge alternative interpretations (C39), showing appropriate scientific caution. The statistical approach controls for multiple comparisons.

results.result: Target memory decoding in non-competitive conditions showed significant above-chance performance 2.55-2.92s post-cue (pcluster<0.05), later than typical reinstatement windows. In the competitive condition, cue-locked decoding was less robust and did not survive multiple comparison correction, but response-locked analysis revealed significant target classification ~200ms before the button press, with stronger classification on correct versus incorrect trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C47 demonstrate successful memory decoding with appropriate controls and statistical corrections. The response-locked analysis (C44-C47) addresses the limitation of temporal variability in the cue-locked analysis, providing converging evidence. The relationship between decoding strength and behavioral accuracy (C45) validates the classifier's sensitivity to memory processes.

results.result: Across retrieval repetitions, target memory decodability increased significantly from first to third recall (pcluster<0.05, 1.79-2.11s), while competitor decodability showed a numerical but non-significant decrease. A significant repetition-by-associate interaction (F(1,20)=5.187, p=0.034) revealed target strengthening (first: 49.43%, third: 53.14%, t(20)=-2.46, p=0.02) and non-significant competitor weakening. Stronger competitor reactivation (0-1s post-cue) correlated with higher initial intrusion rates (r=0.446, p=0.04).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 show mixed support for the hypothesis of target strengthening and competitor weakening. While target strengthening is statistically significant, competitor weakening is not (C49, C51), which only partially supports the predictions. The correlation between competitor reactivation and intrusions (C53) provides supporting evidence, but the overall pattern deviates from pre-registered predictions. The third repetition comparison to chance shows marginal significance (pcluster=0.07).

results.result: Target memories can be decoded from MEG signals in non-competitive conditions, while under interference, target reactivation is less robust initially but increases over repetitions. This pattern could emerge from target strengthening or reduced competitor interference. Response-locked analysis revealed that temporal variance in memory reactivation explains the weaker cue-locked results.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 provide a coherent summary of the decoding results with appropriate acknowledgment of alternative explanations (C56). The response-locked analysis (C57) addresses a methodological limitation and strengthens the interpretation. However, C56 correctly notes that the mechanism remains ambiguous between target strengthening and competitor weakening.

results.result: IRASA analysis identified 3 Hz as the dominant frequency for both target and competitor memory reactivation in the competitive condition, with power exceeding the 95th percentile of surrogate-label classifiers. Non-competitive conditions showed slightly faster peaks (4-5 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 demonstrate appropriate frequency analysis using IRASA to separate oscillatory from fractal components. The use of surrogate-label classifiers provides a proper statistical baseline. The descriptive difference between CC (3 Hz) and NC (4-5 Hz) conditions is noted but not formally tested statistically.

results.result: Fidelity values for both target and competitor memories were significantly modulated by the hippocampal 3 Hz theta rhythm, with the third retrieval repetition showing significant modulation exceeding the 95th percentile.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 demonstrate phase-amplitude coupling between memory reactivation and hippocampal theta using appropriate modulation index analysis with empirical chance distributions. The finding that modulation is significant specifically in the third repetition aligns with the hypothesis of evolving phase separation over time.

results.result: In the third retrieval repetition, target and competitor memories showed significant phase separation with a mean angular difference of 34° (Rayleigh test: z(20)=5.03, p=0.005), significantly different from zero (z(20)=8.48, p=0.004). No significant phase separation was found in earlier repetitions or when averaging across all repetitions. This finding partly confirms the hypothesis that competing memories become increasingly separated along the hippocampal theta rhythm, though it deviates from the pre-registered expectation of separation throughout the recall phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 provide the key evidence for the main hypothesis using appropriate circular statistics (Rayleigh tests). The finding of phase separation specifically in the third repetition is statistically robust. However, the authors appropriately note (C68) that finding separation only in the last repetition deviates from pre-registered predictions, and the lack of significant difference between first and third repetitions (C67) weakens the claim of progressive separation.

results.result: Participants were split by intrusion score into high- and low-intrusion groups. The high-intrusion group showed a mean phase separation of 7° (not significantly different from zero, z(9)=1.77, p=0.17), while the low-intrusion group showed 57° separation (significantly clustered, z(9)=3.74, p=0.02, but not significantly different from zero, z(9)=3.32, p=0.069). Direct comparison between groups was non-significant (Z=43, p=0.85). This suggests that only low-intrusion participants exhibit significant phase separation, relating neural differentiation to behavioral performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 present an interesting post-hoc analysis relating phase separation to behavior, but the results are mixed. The low-intrusion group shows clustering around 57° but fails to reach significance for deviation from zero (p=0.069). The direct group comparison is non-significant (C75), and the analysis is underpowered with only 10 participants per group. The interpretation (C76) is reasonable but not strongly supported statistically.

results.result: Cross-correlation analysis revealed a significant cluster starting ~1s post-cue with a maximum lag of 30° phase angle between target and competitor reactivation, suggesting competitor reactivation lags behind targets. Analysis of continuous fidelity timecourses filtered at 3 Hz showed a consistent lag of approximately 45° between competing memories. These analyses provide converging evidence for temporal segregation during the last retrieval repetition.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 provide complementary analyses supporting phase separation using different methods (cross-correlation and phase subtraction). The convergence between methods (30° and 45° lags) strengthens confidence in the finding. These analyses were not pre-registered but appropriately address the same hypothesis from different analytical perspectives.

results.result: The study demonstrates that neural signatures of competing memories become increasingly phase separated along the theta rhythm, with a 34° phase shift in the third repetition. Larger phase differences were associated with fewer intrusion errors (57° in low-intrusion vs. 7° in high-intrusion participants). Both target and competitor memories showed significant 3 Hz phase modulation, and cross-correlation suggested a 30° phase lag. These findings largely confirm predictions from the oscillating interference resolution model, supporting a role for slow oscillations in temporally segregating interfering memories.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C90 provide an appropriate summary of the main findings. The evidence for phase separation is statistically robust (C85), though the behavioral correlation (C87) has limitations noted above. The authors appropriately acknowledge deviations from pre-registered hypotheses (C90) while maintaining that the results largely support the model. The convergence of multiple analyses (phase-locking, cross-correlation, modulation index) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that repeated recall enhances retrieved memories and induces forgetting of non-retrieved competitors, with fMRI evidence for up- and downregulation of neural target and competitor patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 accurately cite relevant prior work (Karpicke & Roediger 2008, Rowland 2014, Anderson et al. 1994, Kuhl et al. 2007, Wimber et al. 2015) to establish the theoretical context. These are appropriately characterized as prior findings not tested in the current study.

results.result: The study found neural evidence for target strengthening and competitor weakening within the maximum reactivation window, though target strengthening was more robust. Competitor reactivation was more evident on incorrect trials. The relatively stable competitor reactivation might reflect the lack of feedback in the task. Overall, results suggest MEG can track dynamic changes in overlapping memories.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 provide a balanced interpretation of the strengthening/weakening results, appropriately noting that competitor weakening was less robust (C95) and offering a plausible explanation (C97). The citation to recent EEG work (Bramão et al. 2022) appropriately contextualizes the findings. The interpretation is cautious and acknowledges limitations.

results.result: Decoding in the competitive condition was less robust than in non-competitive conditions, likely due to temporal variance in memory recall across trials and participants. Previous work suggests theta phase is reset by memory cues and remains stationary, so memory reactivation should be most coherent when aligned to cue onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 provide appropriate methodological context and justification for the cue-locked analysis approach. The citations to prior work (Rizzuto et al. 2006, Ter Wal et al. 2021) support the rationale. The acknowledgment of temporal variance (C100) is important for interpreting the weaker CC decoding results.

results.result: The theta-gamma model proposes that gamma bursts coupled to theta phases provide timing for ordering items in working memory, with theta modulating excitability and feedback inhibition organizing firing sequences. Human studies support this theta-gamma code. Both the oscillating interference resolution model and theta-gamma models share the assumption that slow oscillations regulate excitation-inhibition balance, though they differ in scope: theta-gamma models address ongoing high load states, while the oscillating interference resolution model is a learning model oriented toward optimizing future network states.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C112 accurately describe the theta-gamma model and its relationship to the oscillating interference resolution model, with appropriate citations (Lisman & Idiart 1995, Lisman & Jensen 2013, Buzsáki 2006, Norman et al. 2006). The distinction between the models' theoretical scopes is clearly articulated and helps contextualize the current findings.

results.result: Prior human intracranial work showed that neural representations of interfering spatial goal locations couple to distinct theta phases, and phase precession occurs during navigation. The current results directly support that phase coding can temporally separate competing memory representations in humans and suggest this code adaptively evolves across repeated retrievals.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 appropriately contextualize the findings within prior human intracranial work (Kunz et al. 2019, Qasim et al. 2021, Watrous et al. 2018) and draw reasonable inferences from the current data. The claim that the code "adaptively evolves" (C116) is supported by the finding of phase separation specifically in later repetitions.

results.result: A second computational model proposes that encoding and retrieval operations occur at opposing theta phases. The current finding of 35-57° phase separation is consistent with both targets and competitors reactivating during the retrieval portion of the theta cycle with sufficient separation for differentiation. However, the oscillating interference resolution model predicts up to 180° separation across the full cycle. The two models may be compatible given that encoding and retrieval occur in different hippocampal subcircuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C122 thoughtfully address the relationship between the current findings and competing theoretical frameworks (Hasselmo et al. 2002, Kunec et al. 2005). The authors appropriately note the discrepancy between observed phase separation (35-57°) and the oscillating interference resolution model's prediction (180°), while offering a potential reconciliation (C122). This demonstrates appropriate scientific reasoning about theoretical implications.

results.result: The non-monotonic plasticity hypothesis predicts that strong competitors co-activating in the high-inhibition phase will be integrated via LTP, while moderately co-active competitors will be differentiated via LTD. The current data support that low temporal separation (7° in high-intrusion group) relates to integration and higher intrusions, while larger separation (57° in low-intrusion group) relates to differentiation and lower interference. Temporal separation could be a prerequisite for spatial differentiation, though this remains speculative.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C135 present an interesting theoretical interpretation linking temporal (phase) separation to spatial (representational) differentiation, with appropriate citations to fMRI work (Hulbert & Norman 2015, Ritvo et al. 2019, etc.). However, the interpretation is largely speculative (C128, C133, C134, C135) and the statistical support for the behavioral correlation is weak (as noted in the evaluation of C70-C76). The study was not designed to test spatial differentiation directly.

results.result: Previous studies show large variations in human theta frequency, with the current study finding 3-4 Hz in the competitive condition versus 4-5 Hz in non-competitive conditions. Prior work shows theta slows with memory load, consistent with the theoretical idea that slower rhythms accommodate better phase separation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C141 appropriately contextualize the frequency findings with extensive prior literature (Goyal et al. 2020, Kerrén et al. 2018, Ter Wal et al. 2021, Fell et al. 2011, Wolinski et al. 2018, Lisman & Idiart 1995, Lisman & Jensen 2013). The descriptive observation of slower theta in CC versus NC (C141) is consistent with the load-dependent slowing hypothesis, though this was not formally tested statistically.

results.result: Phase coding offers a theoretical solution for temporally segregating interfering information, with prior evidence from spatial navigation work. The current study demonstrates that phase coding facilitates separation of overlapping associative memories, offering a possible mechanism for resolving competition between simultaneously active memories. These findings add to literature showing slow oscillations orchestrate neural processing with observable behavioral effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 provide an appropriate concluding synthesis of the work's contributions. The claims appropriately acknowledge prior work (C143) while clearly stating the novel contribution (C144). The broader implications (C145-C146) are reasonable given the evidence presented, though appropriately cautious in characterizing the mechanism as "possible" rather than definitively established.
